newsitem.title: USA: Lott says balanced budget legislation is close.
newsitem.headline: Lott says balanced budget legislation is close.

text.p: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott Saturday accused the Clinton administration of playing politics with balanced-budget legislation through "fanciful" public statements and "contrived" private data.
Still, the Mississippi Republican was optimistic about the outlook for agreement on final tax and spending bills to implement a five-year balanced budget pact with the White House.
"But you know the old saying: Close, but no cigar. Any celebration at this point would definitely be premature," he said in the Republican response to President Clinton's radio address.
Republicans have set Aug. 1 as the deadline for passing the legislation. After that date, Congress is scheduled to adjourn for a month-long recess.
As Republicans sped up the budget talks, meeting late into the night and during the weekend, some Democrats tried to apply the brakes, warning Clinton not to rush into a deal.

Led by New York Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, Democrats on the influential Senate Finance Committee asked Clinton to defer final action until the fall if necessary in order to work out legislation that met party priorities.

They predicted the federal budget deficit could shrink to about $30 billion at the close of fiscal 1997, which ends Sept. 30. If current trends continued, the budget could be in balance next year without new action by Congress.
But Lott urged action before the congressional recess, saying: "By this time next week, the world will know whether we have succeeded. I'm betting ... that we do."
He appealed to Clinton to say publicly that he would sign legislation sent to him in the coming days.

"We have compromised with him. We have both given ground and found common ground ... and, if it would make a difference, I will stand in the well of the Senate and whistle 'Hail to the Chief,'" Lott said.
However, he acknowledged that "pinning down this president on a policy decision" was very difficult.
"In almost a quarter-century on Capitol Hill, I have worked with six administrations, both Democrat and Republican. This one, let me tell you, is unique," he said.
The Clinton administration "continues to play politics" with what Lott called the most important piece of legislation to come before Congress in many a year.
"Its public assertions are often fanciful. Its private data are often contrived," he said.
Despite all that, Republicans had reached out to congressional Democrats who had played important roles in advancing the bipartisan legislation, Lott added.
"As of today, the outlook is encouraging," he said.
